title: Single Provider Path Down With No Local Fault (Provider Route Limit)
symptom: A site loses internet or cloud access through one provider. The BGP session to that provider is down or resetting, local interfaces look healthy, and no local change explains it.
checks: Confirm the circuit and interface to the provider are up with no errors.
Check the BGP neighbor state and the last reset reason (e.g., show bgp neighbor). Look for a prefix-limit or maximum-prefix notification.
Count the prefixes we advertise to that provider and compare with the limit in the provider contract or portal.
Check for a recent change that added or advertised new networks.
Check whether a second independent provider path exists and is carrying traffic.
resolution: If a second path exists, confirm traffic moved to it and leave it there.
Open a priority ticket with the provider. Ask which prefix limit they enforce on the session and ask them to raise it or clear the session.
If we advertise more prefixes than needed, ask the on-call engineer to summarize them under the limit through the change process.
Confirm the session is Established and prefixes are exchanged.
Confirm the affected users or app reach their endpoint.
Follow-up: record the provider's limit on the circuit record and add a monitor for advertised prefix count.
escalate_if: There is no second path and the session is still down 15 minutes after the provider ticket is opened.
The provider says no limit was hit.
More than one site is affected.
Include: circuit ID, provider ticket number, neighbor state, last reset reason, prefix count advertised.

title: Both Redundant Circuits Down at the Same Time (Provider Maintenance)
symptom: A site loses most or all outbound paths. Both circuits that should back each other up are down, often with no local fault.
checks: Check provider maintenance notices and the maintenance calendar for every circuit at the site.
Confirm the state of each circuit (up/down, light levels, error counters).
Check whether the site normally depends on another site to advertise its routes.
Find the documented manual backup path for this site.
resolution: If the outage matches a provider maintenance window, ask the provider for the end time and a status update.
Open a ticket if the window has passed and circuits are not back.
If a manual backup path is documented, the on-call engineer decides whether to use it.
When maintenance ends, confirm both circuits are up and routes are advertised again.
Follow-up: ask the provider to schedule maintenance on redundant circuits in separate windows.
escalate_if: Both circuits are down and no maintenance notice explains it.
The maintenance window has ended and either circuit is still down.
Include: both circuit IDs, provider ticket numbers, start time, current state of each.

title: Multicast Packets Dropping on One Port
symptom: Multicast traffic through one switch port is dropped. A downstream system or monitor goes blind and the port's discard counter climbs steadily.
checks: Check input discards and errors on the port. Note whether they are increasing.
Check whether only multicast through that port is affected and other traffic is fine.
Compare the hardware model and software version with the vendor's known-issue list for stuck buffers or input drops.
Check whether the same traffic arrives cleanly through another path.
resolution: If the port carries only this traffic and a redundant path exists, the on-call engineer may shut the interface so traffic uses the other path.
Confirm the downstream system or monitor recovers.
Open a vendor case citing the known issue.
Follow-up: schedule the software upgrade the vendor names as the fix.
escalate_if: There is no redundant path for the traffic.
Discards continue after the port is shut or on other ports.
Include: switch, port, counter values over time, hardware model and software version.

title: Connectivity Lost After Decommissioning or Disconnecting Old Equipment
symptom: Connectivity to an outside office or service drops right after old routers or a temporary bridge connection are shut down or removed.
checks: Identify the exact change that was made and its ticket.
Check which routes the removed device or link was advertising to the provider.
Check whether the new routers advertise those routes on their own.
Check the path to the affected office or service now.
resolution: Revert the change immediately (re-enable the device or link) following the change rollback plan.
Confirm the routes are advertised again and connectivity is restored.
Do not retry the decommissioning until the dependency is mapped and fixed.
Follow-up: list everything that still depends on the old equipment before the next attempt.
escalate_if: The rollback does not restore connectivity.
The change had no rollback plan.
Include: change ticket, what was shut down, which office or service is affected.

title: Storage or Service Down After Switch Replacement (Stale Configuration)
symptom: A service loses connectivity during or just after a switch hardware swap. The replacement switch is up but its paired switch or ports are not working.
checks: Confirm which switch was replaced and why.
Check the configuration the new switch is running and whether it was loaded automatically from a leftover file.
Check the pairing or link state between the new switch and its partner.
Check which ports are down or in the wrong mode.
resolution: Move traffic to unaffected sites or paths if possible.
Disconnect the new switch from the live network if it is not configured correctly.
Have the on-call engineer load the verified standard configuration, then reconnect.
Confirm the pair is healthy and the service is reachable.
Follow-up: require a clean, verified configuration before any replacement switch connects.
escalate_if: The service is down and the correct configuration is not available.
The pair still does not form after the standard configuration is loaded.
Include: switch name and role, change ticket, what configuration was loaded, port states.

title: Playback or Feed Errors After a Router Swap (Link Bundle Mismatch)
symptom: Errors in a broadcast or application feed start shortly after an edge router was replaced. The link to a downstream appliance may show up but not pass traffic correctly.
checks: Confirm what changed (router swapped, vendor changed).
Check the status of the bundle (link aggregation) to the downstream appliance and its member links.
Compare the bundle mode and settings on both ends. They must match.
Check for errors on the member links and on the appliance.
resolution: Correct the bundle settings so both ends match (on-call engineer applies, or the change owner).
Confirm the bundle is up with all members.
Confirm the feed or playback is clean.
Follow-up: add a post-change check of every downstream dependency to the swap procedure.
escalate_if: The bundle is up and the errors continue.
The other end is a vendor-managed appliance and settings cannot be confirmed.
Include: router, appliance, bundle ID, settings on both ends, error symptoms.

title: Multicast Subscriptions Lost After Hardware Migration
symptom: Devices that receive multicast lose their subscriptions after being moved to new network hardware. No error is shown; the streams just do not arrive.
checks: Confirm which devices were moved and when.
Check that multicast routing is enabled on every interface involved on the new hardware, including the receivers' interface.
Check whether the receivers' join requests (IGMP) are seen on the new switch.
Check multicast route state for the group on the new router.
resolution: Have the on-call engineer apply the missing multicast routing setting on the interface.
Test a device joining the group from more than one location.
Confirm the streams are arriving at all moved devices.
Follow-up: add multicast routing to the migration checklist.
escalate_if: Joins are seen but the stream still does not arrive.
More than one interface is missing the setting and the scope is unclear.
Include: group addresses, interfaces, device list, what you checked.

title: Monitoring Dark or Hosts Appear Offline After a Configuration Sync
symptom: Monitoring for a site goes dark or hosts falsely show offline after a configuration management platform resync or sync repair on other devices.
checks: Find what sync or push ran on the platform in the last hour.
Compare the interface configuration on the affected switches with the last backup.
Check whether the missing settings were applied directly on the device and not through the platform.
Check whether the hosts are actually up by another route.
resolution: Stop further syncs on the platform until this is resolved.
Have the on-call engineer restore the lost interface configuration from the network backup system.
Confirm monitoring returns and the hosts show online.
Follow-up: move the restored settings into the platform's templates.
escalate_if: The backup does not contain the missing configuration.
More than one site or device group is affected.
Include: the platform job that ran, affected switches, backup used.

title: Broadcast or Service Feeds Lost After New Switches Added (Duplicate Loopback Address)
symptom: Signals or feeds from a facility are lost, often during a live event, shortly after new leaf switches were deployed.
checks: Find the new switches and when they were deployed.
Compare their loopback addresses with all existing switches and look for duplicates.
Check routing and neighbor tables for the duplicate address pointing to the wrong device.
Confirm the impact (which feeds or services).
resolution: Shut the uplinks of the new switches.
Reassign the new switches to unused loopback addresses from the plan.
Bring the uplinks back and confirm the feeds return.
Follow-up: run the address-in-use check before any new switch is connected.
escalate_if: Feeds do not return after the uplinks are shut.
The duplicate is on devices that are not part of the new deployment.
Include: the duplicated address, both devices, affected feeds, change ticket.

title: New Hosts Reach Each Other but Not Outside Their Virtual Network (Pairing Without a Partner)
symptom: After maintenance, new hosts on a virtual network segment can talk locally but cannot reach anything outside the segment.
checks: Check whether the leaf switches have switch pairing enabled and whether a real partner switch exists.
Check the state of the pairing control interface (down is the symptom).
Check the tunnel or virtual network status on the switches.
Confirm older hosts on the segment still work.
resolution: Have the on-call engineer remove the leftover pairing configuration.
Bring the control interface up if it is still down.
Confirm the new hosts reach destinations outside the segment.
Follow-up: before enabling a feature, confirm the switch is set up the way the feature expects.
escalate_if: Connectivity does not return after the pairing is removed.
Existing hosts are also affected.
Include: switches, segment, control interface state, change ticket.

title: Failover Did Not Work After a Fiber Cut (Asymmetric Routing)
symptom: After a fiber cut or circuit loss, failover does not work cleanly. Traffic leaves by one path and returns by another and firewalls drop it. An emergency reroute can break other regions.
checks: Confirm which circuit is down and whether a repair ticket is open with the provider.
Trace the outbound and return path for an affected flow and check they match.
Check firewall logs for dropped return traffic.
List any emergency routing change made and which regions it touches.
resolution: The on-call engineer forces traffic onto the single healthy path.
Check every other region for missing routes after the change.
Announce any missing routes the forced path needs.
When the fiber is repaired, revert the emergency change and confirm paths are symmetric.
Follow-up: remove temporary workarounds rather than leaving them in place.
escalate_if: Any region loses reachability after the reroute.
Failover does not complete within 10 minutes.
Include: circuit and ticket, affected regions, paths traced, firewall drop evidence.

title: Publishing or Service Connectivity Lost During Migration (Leaked Specific Route)
symptom: A platform loses connectivity during a migration or after a routing edit. A more specific route appears from a legacy network and pulls traffic the wrong way.
checks: Find any routing change made in the last hour, including ones outside the change process.
Check the route to the platform's address and the prefix that is winning.
Check which device is advertising that prefix.
Confirm the platform's expected path.
resolution: Revert the routing edit that created the route.
Confirm the unwanted route has disappeared.
Confirm the platform is reachable.
Follow-up: any troubleshooting change on a live device needs approval first.
escalate_if: You cannot find who made the edit.
The route remains after the revert.
Include: the prefix, the device advertising it, change ticket if any.

title: Two Sites Isolated With the Primary Link Already Down (Last Path Lost)
symptom: Connectivity between two distant sites is completely down. One link was already out awaiting repair and the remaining path has just failed, often during maintenance.
checks: List every path between the two sites and the status of each, including long-running repairs.
Check for planned maintenance on the surviving path.
Check with the provider for the state of the surviving path and its equipment.
Confirm the scope (which services are cut).
resolution: If maintenance is in progress on the surviving path, ask the provider to stop or finish it.
Ask the provider to restore the path remotely.
If remote restore fails, ask for on-site help (equipment power cycle or repair).
Confirm both sites reach each other over the restored path.
Follow-up: do not let a temporary single path stay in place.
escalate_if: No path is available.
The provider cannot restore it within 30 minutes.
Include: all path IDs and states, provider tickets, maintenance notices.

title: Data Center Unreachable After a Routing Policy Change (Prefixes Not Advertised)
symptom: A data center loses internet and cloud connectivity and many services show errors. The problem may appear minutes after the change, when it looked fine at first.
checks: Find the latest policy change and its ticket.
Check whether the site's own prefixes are still advertised to the outside (look at what is sent to the neighbors).
Compare the policy with the previous version for redistribution or static route differences.
Check again a few minutes after any change, since the effect can be delayed.
resolution: Revert both routers to the previous configuration (rollback plan).
Confirm the site's prefixes are visible externally.
Confirm error rates return to normal.
Follow-up: wait several minutes after this kind of change before closing the check.
escalate_if: Reverting does not restore advertisement.
The change had no rollback plan.
Include: routers, change ticket, prefixes expected versus advertised.

title: Live Feeds Degraded or Missing (A and B Feeds Share a Dependency)
symptom: Live events lose picture fully or partly. The A and B feeds that should back each other up are both affected, and recorded archives may show gaps.
checks: Check whether maintenance is under way at the facility originating the feeds.
Check the A and B paths to each destination and note what they share.
Check whether destinations are reconnecting at once through the same recovery path.
Check the archive for gaps.
resolution: Stabilize the shared recovery path (the on-call engineer limits or staggers the reconnects).
Confirm both feeds are clean at each destination.
Check that archives are recording.
Follow-up: review the A and B paths end to end for any shared device or path.
escalate_if: Either feed is still degraded after 15 minutes.
A live event is affected.
Include: events affected, facility, which feeds and destinations, maintenance ticket.

title: Playback Problems and Timing Alerts After Link Cleanup (Timing Protocol Paths Removed)
symptom: Streaming or playback problems and timing alerts appear after a network cleanup removed links that looked redundant.
checks: Find the cleanup change and which links it removed.
Check whether the removed links carried precision timing traffic.
Check the timing alerts for when they started and compare with the change time.
Check whether the remaining paths can carry timing traffic.
resolution: Revert the cleanup (rollback plan) to restore the links.
Confirm timing alerts clear.
Confirm playback is back to normal.
Follow-up: preserve dedicated timing paths before any more cleanup.
escalate_if: Alerts continue after the revert.
Timing sources are not locked.
Include: change ticket, links removed, alerts and times.

title: Load Balancers Crashing Repeatedly (Debug Logging Memory Bug)
symptom: Load balancer service engines restart or crash again and again over days. Often only one newly created group is affected.
checks: Confirm which service engine group is affected and when the crashes began.
Compare the group's settings with a stable group, looking for missing safeguards.
Check the crash logs and the memory used for debug and trace logging.
Check the vendor's known-issue list for the software version.
resolution: Have the on-call engineer lower the debug and trace logging memory setting to the minimum.
Watch the group for a day to confirm the crashes stop.
Open or update a vendor case.
Follow-up: plan the software upgrade the vendor recommends and check new groups inherit standard settings.
escalate_if: Crashes continue after the setting change.
Other groups start crashing.
Include: group, crash times, logs, software version, setting values.

title: Live Channels Off the Air After a Circuit Change
symptom: Publishing for many live channels stops right after a change to a network circuit at a data center.
checks: Find the circuit change and its ticket.
Check which channels and services use that circuit.
Check the circuit state and routes after the change.
Check where the channels can publish instead.
resolution: Revert the circuit change as soon as the impact is clear.
Confirm the channels return and publishing counts are normal.
If channels are slow to return, move the busiest to a healthier data center.
Follow-up: check what rides on a circuit before changing it.
escalate_if: Channels do not return after the revert.
The number of affected channels is growing.
Include: change ticket, circuit, channel count, time of impact.

title: Several Tools Failing at Once After a BGP Drop on a Legacy Router
symptom: Several unrelated systems fail together, including deployment and login tools. All of them reach the cloud through one older router whose BGP sessions have dropped without an error.
checks: Check the BGP sessions on the router (down since when, last reset reason).
Check whether the failing tools share the router as their only path to the cloud.
Check the router's firmware version against the vendor's known-bug list.
Treat the pages as one incident and avoid separate fixes.
resolution: Recover the sessions (the on-call engineer clears or restarts them).
Confirm the dependent tools, including deployments and login, work again.
Open a vendor case if the cause is unclear.
Follow-up: patch or isolate old hardware even when it is due for retirement.
escalate_if: Sessions do not come back.
The drop repeats.
Include: router, firmware version, session state, list of failing tools.
